_meta.schema: entry: id, tool, explain_tool?, privilege?, category, intent, rhel_versions{7,8,9,10}, flags[], verify, undo, blast, stig[], source, verified — ADR-001 §5.1
_meta.explain_tool_rule: Optional. Set only when the entry is filed under tool as the subject the operator is asking about, but every rhel_versions command actually invokes a DIFFERENT binary (e.g. firewalld-service-active is filed under firewall-cmd for navigation, but emits systemctl). When present, the inspector and the G1 gate resolve flag explanations and the tool/binary-agreement check through explain_tool instead of tool. tool still drives the sidebar Tools rail and stays the subject; explain_tool never changes what the operator sees, only which dictionary answers the flag panel (Marcus Reed Panels review PANEL-001 / condition G1).
_meta.privilege_rule: Optional, one of extract/schema.py's PRIVILEGES ("root" today). Set when the entry's OWN assembled command needs elevated privilege to run on a STIG'd host that the command text itself never requests (no sudo/su in the template) -- distinct from blast, which rates what the command DOES once it runs, not what it takes to run it. The UI shows a privilege badge next to blast and the evidence exporter records a Requires: line, so the content validation protocol's safety rule (no sudo used during a capture run) can defer the entry correctly instead of silently skipping it (G4(e); gen-sshd-test-config, sshd_config not world-readable on defiant/saratoga, CR-T-34).
_meta.status: CR-T-02 skeleton (3 curated entries) + CR-T-17..25 generator specs (24 entries): guided forms for firewall-cmd, nmcli, journalctl, lvm, sshd, useradd/usermod, systemctl, dnf/yum, semanage/setsebool, chage, auditctl/ausearch, rsyslog, chronyd, podman. Full catalog authoring is still CR-T-33.

entries.notes: H1 correction (Marcus Reed): this entry was wrongly raised to blast yellow at G4(d) on a misreading of -Q as clock-stepping (Caleb Stone's CR-T-34 note read -Q for -q; Eli Cross's ruling and this branch's previous commit both repeated it). chronyd(8) draws a clear line between the two: -q is the mode that actually adjusts the system time and then quits (content-src/raw/rhel8/chronyd.man.txt#L64-L66, identical at rhel10#L64-L66); -Q behaves the same way except for that one adjustment -- it reports the measured offset and, because it skips opening network ports entirely, can run as a non-root user as long as nothing in the config needs elevated access (#L68-L74, identical at rhel10#L68-L74). This toolkit only ever generates -Q. blast restored to green. MCR-SEC-025: chronyd(8) SYNOPSIS is `chronyd [OPTION]... [DIRECTIVE]...` (#L7, identical at rhel10#L7), so configuration directives are OPERANDS accepted after the options, and -Q itself takes no argument (#L68). The directive is a separate word after -Q, never -Q's value. RHEL 7 uses chronyd by default for NTP (chrony package). The legacy ntpd daemon is available as an alternative from the separate ntp package but is not installed or enabled by default on any pinned release (RHEL 7 System Administrator's Guide, ch. 18-19) -- chronyd is the only NTP daemon this toolkit generates commands for.

entries.intent: Mount an NFS share, now and at boot

9.notes: showmount -e lists what the server exports (needs nfs-utils). _netdev in fstab makes boot wait for the network before mounting - without it, boots race the network and land in emergency mode. SELinux gotcha: services reading NFS content often need a boolean (getsebool -a | grep nfs). Grey Beard shipped this as a four-line block (showmount -e, mkdir, mount, an fstab append, findmnt --verify). MD CODE RED ships one command per entry, so the mount itself is the command and the rest of the sequence is here: showmount -e SERVER lists the exports (nfs-utils), mkdir -p the mountpoint first, then add the fstab line with _netdev and re-run findmnt --verify. The server address shown is TEST-NET-1 (RFC 5737), not a real host. Carried across from the Grey Beard Ansible field kit (same owner, orbit/grey-beard-ansible), which is single-version and was authored and used on RHEL 9: this is the RHEL 9 row, and the other releases repeat it unchanged. entries.intent: Cap the journal's disk usage permanently (after a cleanup)

9.notes: The disk-full tree says it: don't just delete - cap. --vacuum-size=500M does the one-time cleanup; the drop-in makes the cap permanent so the appointment never recurs. Drop-in beats editing journald.conf directly (survives updates). Grey Beard shipped this as a four-line block: measure with --disk-usage, write a /etc/systemd/journald.conf.d/size.conf drop-in with SystemMaxUse=500M, restart systemd-journald. The one-time reclaim is the command here. The permanent cap is the drop-in, and it is the half that stops the appointment recurring - a drop-in rather than an edit to journald.conf, so a package update does not take it back. entries.intent: Stop a runaway process, gently then firmly

9.notes: Plain kill sends SIGTERM - a polite 'clean up and exit'. -9 (SIGKILL) is uncatchable: no cleanup, possible corrupted state. If it's a service, systemctl stop is the right door, not kill. Mentor: kill -9 first is like unplugging the server to close a program. It's on the Forbidden List as a habit; as a last resort it's a tool. Grey Beard wrote this with a <pid> placeholder and an inline shell comment carrying the kill -9 escalation. Both are removed: a shipped command with a placeholder in it is a command someone runs with the placeholder still in it, and a second command hidden behind a '#' is a second command. 1234 stands in for the pid you read from ps. The escalation is `kill -9 PID`, and only after SIGTERM has been ignored. entries.intent: Restore from a tar backup - safely, to a staging area first

9.notes: List first (-t), extract into a STAGING directory (-C), diff against live, then copy over only what you mean to restore. Never extract an absolute-path archive as root onto / - one wrong archive overwrites the living system. --strip-components=N trims leading path levels when needed. Mentor: A backup that has never been restore-tested is a rumor. This staging pattern IS the restore test - run it before you need it. Grey Beard shipped this as a four-line staging drill: list with -t, mkdir the staging directory, extract into it with -C, diff the staged tree against live. The extraction is the command. Do not skip the other three: list before you trust an archive, stage before you restore, and diff before you copy anything back over a living system.
